description.narrative: Nipah virus is a deadly bat-borne virus that can cause severe respiratory infections and encephalitis. Outbreaks are rare, but have a high fatality rate (up to 75%), and primarily occur in Bangladesh and India. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) plays a crucial role in combating Nipah virus by funding the development and trial of vaccines. CEPI is currently supporting the development of two potential vaccines. One (ChAdOx1 NipahB vaccine) has received support from the European Medicines Agency's PRIority MEdicines (PRIME) scheme and is currently completing its Phase 1 trial (assessing vaccine dose, safety and tolerability in humans). The second (PHV02 vaccine) is about to start Phase 2 clinical trials in Bangladesh (evaluating broader safety, dose optimisation, manufacturability and stockpiling strategy). These efforts are part of CEPI's mandate to counter epidemic and pandemic threats, ensuring that vaccines are developed and made available to address potential outbreaks like Nipah in our region.

With support from the Australian Government, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) has supported the development of the first-ever chikungunya vaccine. Chikungunya virus is an emerging global threat, spread through mosquitos with recent transmission occurring in a number of countries in the Indo-Pacific. Climate change is expanding the habitable regions of the transmitting mosquitoes, putting a growing population at risk of infection. ‍ Chikungunya virus can cause sudden and large outbreaks with high attack rates of the population where the virus is circulating; once infected people experience acute fever, headaches, nausea, debilitating and chronic joint pain. In late 2023 – for the first time ever – a CEPI-supported‍ chikungunya vaccine received regulatory approval from Food and Drug Administration (USA), followed by European approval (May 2024). This represents a significant scientific and public health milestone - a licensed chikungunya vaccine available to address unmet medical need.
